title: Iran-Linked Hackers Suspected in Coordinated Attack on U.S. Water Systems
excerpt: U.S. investigators point to Iranian-affiliated group CyberAv3ngers after more than 30 Minnesota water systems were targeted in cyberattacks that prompted a federal warning about escalating threats to critical infrastructure.
body:
• U.S. officials suspect Iranian-linked hackers behind coordinated cyberattacks on more than 30 community water systems in Minnesota on July 26-27.
  • The FBI says water utilities in at least seven states have reported hacking incidents, with some attacks degrading water operations and causing loss of pressure.
  • CISA issued an urgent warning urging water system operators to disconnect internet-facing equipment, citing password changes that locked out operators and triggered boil-water notices.
  • Security firm Tenable linked the attack pattern to CyberAv3ngers, a group the U.S. government says is a front for Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.

U.S. investigators have concluded that Iranian-linked hackers were likely behind a wave of cyberattacks that struck more than 30 municipal water systems across Minnesota this week, according to a New York Times report confirmed by multiple federal officials. The attacks, which targeted wells, treatment plants, and automated control systems on July 26 and 27, mark a significant escalation in cyber threats to American critical infrastructure amid the ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict.

The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) responded Thursday with an urgent advisory warning water and wastewater system operators nationwide to immediately disconnect internet-facing equipment from their networks. The FBI disclosed that water utilities in at least seven states have reported incidents, with some attacks "degrading water operations."

What Happened in Minnesota

The coordinated attack targeted programmable logic controllers (PLCs) and operator interface screens used to remotely monitor and control water infrastructure. The most severe incident hit the 1,700-person community of Braham, where hackers disabled the well and water treatment plant's computerized controls for approximately two hours.

https://x.com/MOSSADil/status/2082953129927245936

Plymouth's IT division preemptively disconnected cellular-connected equipment at two water towers and multiple wastewater stations. South St. Paul reported compromised automated utility controls, and Maple Plain declared a local state of emergency. In all confirmed cases, officials said water quality was never compromised.

"This attack on critical public infrastructure should be a warning to policymakers in St. Paul. Minnesota's local governments are expected to defend essential systems against foreign adversaries and sophisticated criminals, often with limited staff, aging technology and inadequate resources."

— Nate George, Mayor of Braham

However, CISA's broader warning painted a more alarming picture beyond Minnesota. Unidentified victims reported to the FBI that attack effects included loss of water pressure and flooding. In some cases, hackers changed passwords to lock operators out of their own systems, resulting in boil-water notices and forcing communities into sustained manual operations.

The Iran Connection

Tenable, the cybersecurity firm investigating roughly 30 of the Minnesota attacks, stopped short of explicit attribution but said the attack pattern was "consistent" with the group known as CyberAv3ngers — which the U.S. government identifies as a front for the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps Cyber-Electronic Command.

Cynthia Kaiser, a former senior FBI cybersecurity official now with security firm Halcyon, told Reuters that the Minnesota attacks were highly likely a continuation of prior Iranian-affiliated targeting of PLCs and other critical infrastructure documented in a CISA advisory issued in April.

"The fact that a new advisory came out is really indicative of either a broadening of the campaign, new technical details or a renewal of the activity, and probably a combination of all those things."

— Cynthia Kaiser, former senior FBI cybersecurity official

That April advisory, updated on July 22, expanded the scope of targeted devices to include equipment from Schneider Electric and Siemens, beyond the initially tracked Rockwell Automation controllers. Chris Day, public sector chief technical officer at Tenable, described the Minnesota incidents as an "interesting escalation" over prior events.

Escalating Cyber Conflict

The water system attacks come amid an intensification of hostilities between the U.S. and Iran, with both sides trading missile strikes and threatening further escalation. Iranian-linked hacking activity targeting U.S. water facilities predates the current conflict, but affiliated groups have carried out a series of prominent cyberattacks on domestic targets in recent months, including medical services company Stryker and the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority in March.

John Israel, Minnesota's chief information security officer, said the state has "provided relevant information to the federal government, which is evaluating this activity in the broader national context and leading efforts to determine whether it can be attributed to a specific threat actor." Emily Zimmer, a spokesperson for Minnesota IT Services, added that the attacks' "timing, methods of access, and targeted infrastructure share characteristics with other coordinated cyber incidents" observed by federal partners.

A Systemic Vulnerability

The attacks have renewed scrutiny of a long-standing problem: America's water infrastructure remains dangerously exposed to cyber threats. Many municipal water systems operate with outdated technology, minimal cybersecurity staff, and limited budgets. The Environmental Protection Agency has previously warned about vulnerabilities in water and wastewater systems, but progress on hardening these networks has been slow.

Cybersecurity experts warn that artificial intelligence is accelerating the threat. "The threat actors are now using AI to find attack vectors that weren't as easily discoverable before," cybersecurity expert Eric Brown told Fox 9. For now, CISA's advice to water operators is blunt: take internet-connected control systems offline immediately.
nri_angle: Indian-American communities concentrated in Minnesota's Twin Cities metro, home to a significant tech workforce, face the same water infrastructure vulnerabilities exposed by the attacks.
